Yes, it uses non‑ionising sound; it is the preferred tool for fetal and placental assessment.

exam: A 45‑year‑old HIV‑positive man presents with unilateral leg swelling; Doppler shows non‑compressible femoral vein – what is the next management step? — Initiate anticoagulation, arrange follow‑up Doppler in 1‑2 weeks.
You obtain a carotid duplex with PSV 250 cm/s; how does this influence stroke risk and treatment? — Indicates ≥70 % stenosis; start antiplatelet therapy and refer for possible endarterectomy.

A pregnant woman with malaria has an umbilical artery RI of 0.85; what does this suggest? — High resistance flow, possible placental insufficiency; increase fetal monitoring and consider antimalarial therapy.

During renal Doppler, you see a tardus‑parvus waveform; what does it mean and what is your next step? — Downstream low‑velocity, high‑resistance pattern suggesting proximal stenosis; control BP and arrange vascular imaging.

A patient with sickle cell disease has a painful leg; Doppler shows normal arterial flow but sluggish venous flow – how does this guide care? — Suggests vaso‑occlusive crisis; treat pain, hydrate, and monitor; no anticoagulation needed.

Explain why an angle of insonation >60° can lead to underestimation of stenosis severity. — The cosine correction factor decreases, reducing calculated velocity, potentially missing critical narrowing.
ai.title: Doppler Ultrasound in Clinical Practice
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Doppler ultrasound uses sound waves to assess blood flow, helping diagnose vascular and organ pathology. It is portable, affordable, and vital in low‑resource settings.

b: Portable machines cost $5‑10k, feasible in many African hospitals
Can be combined with B‑mode imaging (duplex) for anatomy + flow
sections.p: Doppler ultrasound measures frequency shifts caused by moving red blood cells, providing real‑time flow direction, velocity, and pattern. It can be performed with handheld probes, making it suitable for bedside use.

b: Peak systolic velocity (PSV) reflects maximal arterial flow
Resistive index (RI = (PSV‑EDV)/PSV) helps differentiate stenosis from occlusion
sections.p: Understanding the Doppler shift, aliasing, and waveform interpretation is essential. Waveforms differ by vessel type (arterial vs venous) and downstream resistance.

b: Detects DVT in lower limbs when compression ultrasound unavailable
Assesses carotid stenosis before stroke in hypertensive or HIV patients
Monitors fetal umbilical flow in malaria‑affected pregnancies
sections.p: Doppler guides diagnosis and management of common low‑resource conditions such as deep vein thrombosis (DVT), peripheral arterial disease (PAD), sickle‑cell vaso‑occlusion, and obstetric complications.
When a Doppler machine is unavailable, rely on clinical scores (e.g., Wells for DVT) and basic bedside signs.

t.b: Is there a thrombus? – Absence of compressibility or absent flow confirms DVT, prompting anticoagulation.
What is the degree of stenosis? – PSV > 230 cm/s suggests ≥70 % stenosis; guides referral for endarterectomy.
Is renal artery narrowing present? – PSV > 180 cm/s with tardus‑parvus pattern indicates significant stenosis.
Is fetal placental perfusion adequate? – Elevated systolic/diastolic ratio > 3 suggests placental insufficiency, need close monitoring.

b: DVT – start low‑molecular‑weight heparin; repeat Doppler if symptoms persist.
Severe carotid stenosis – refer for surgical or endovascular intervention; use antiplatelet therapy.
Renal artery stenosis – control hypertension, consider ACE‑inhibitor; re‑image after 3‑6 months.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first; Doppler findings direct therapy intensity and monitoring.

b: Identify waveform pattern that distinguishes arterial from venous flow.
Know the PSV cut‑off for ≥70 % carotid stenosis (≈230 cm/s).
Explain why compression Doppler is preferred over venography in DVT.
sections.p: Examiners love scenario‑based questions linking Doppler findings to next steps.

b: Assuming high velocity always means stenosis – can be due to hyperdynamic state.
Failing to adjust angle of insonation; >60° underestimates velocity.
Relying on a single view; always obtain longitudinal and transverse planes.
sections.p: Errors often arise from mis‑interpreting aliasing or ignoring clinical context.

whenToSeekHelp: Acute limb ischemia with pain, pallor, pulselessness – urgent vascular surgery.
Sudden severe headache with abnormal cerebral Doppler – possible intracranial bleed.
